chapters.title: Three ways to run one circuit

claims.claim: The lab measures steady-state CPU execution on one unchanged input, to see what each call allocates and copies; it does not measure event processing, GPU work, compilation or browser frames.

sources.label: lab/runtime-cost/README.md line 9
sources.quote: The purpose is to measure simple allocation and output-copying costs

sources.label: lab/runtime-cost/README.md line 5
sources.quote: This is steady-state CPU execution on an unchanged input, not event processing, GPU execution, compilation, or a browser frame benchmark.

claims.claim: The report compares three runners: literal reference execution, the tensor executor returning a full wire array, and the tensor executor with reusable buffers returning only the requested outputs.

sources.label: lab/runtime-cost/README.md line 3
sources.quote: compares literal reference execution, the existing tensor executor returning a full wire array, and the tensor executor with reusable buffers returning only requested outputs

claims.claim: The reference runner allocates one fresh array on every call, sized for every source cell plus every operation, and then evaluates each operation as its own scalar step.
The plain tensor executor creates a new workspace on every call, runs the layers, and then allocates a full-width array to hold every wire.
The reusable evaluator allocates its workspace once, when it is created, plus one output array of the requested roots' length; each call runs the layers and copies out only those roots.
The reusable evaluator's output array is overwritten by the next call, so a caller that keeps a frame has to copy the output first.

sources.label: src/runtime/numeric-ui-core.ts line 756
sources.quote: The returned output array is reused and overwritten on the next call.

sources.label: lab/runtime-cost/README.md line 7
sources.quote: Callers that retain a frame must copy the output.

claims.claim: All three paths check every source value against its declared range on every call, so that check is part of every timing and not a difference between them.
The harness warms each method up 200 times, rotates the method order between samples, takes the median of seven samples, and throws if the checksums of the outputs disagree.

sources.label: lab/runtime-cost/README.md line 5
sources.quote: Each measurement reports the median of seven samples, rotates method order, warms each method, and consumes all requested outputs. Checksums must agree across methods.

claims.claim: The test circuit is the HandwiredOS window manager: 234 source cells, 4,646 live operations and 130 layers.

sources.quote: The program has 234 source cells, 4,646 live operations in 130 layers and 9,909 stored weights

claims.claim: In one local run of report.ts (Apple M4 Max, load about 9, not a repo result), the window manager took about 150 µs with the reference, 49 with the full array and 43 with the reusable evaluator.

sources.label: lab/runtime-cost/README.md line 9

claims.claim: On that one run, reusable is about 1.16 times faster than the full array and about 3.5 times faster than the reference; the lab says one ratio is not an architectural guarantee, so these figures are arithmetic on one run, not a result.

chapters.title: What a layer costs by itself

claims.claim: The layer probe measures what a layer costs on the CPU executor, apart from the operations it holds.

sources.label: lab/runtime-cost/layers.ts line 1
sources.quote: What a layer costs on the CPU executor besides its operations

claims.claim: The probe builds 16,384 sums of two terms and arranges them as chains for 64, 1,024 or 16,384 layers.

sources.label: lab/runtime-cost/layers.ts line 1
sources.quote: the same 16,384 sums of two terms

claims.claim: The chain count is the operation count divided by the layer count, so 64 layers run 256 chains side by side and 16,384 layers run one chain of one sum per layer.
Each operation's depth is one more than the deepest thing it reads, and the compiler gives each depth its own layer.
Each layer copies its inputs out of one shared array, does its sparse sums rounding every product and partial sum to a 32-bit float, and then copies its results back.

All three shapes have the same totals: 32,768 input reads, 16,384 outputs and 32,768 stored weights. This follows from the code (each sum reads two inputs and writes one output) and from a local probe; it is not a repo result.
With the totals fixed, the timing gap across the three shapes follows the layer count. The lab shows that correlation and does not test the cause.

sources.label: lab/runtime-cost/layers.ts line 8
sources.quote: Each layer count runs in its own process

claims.claim: Each shape's answer is checked against its exact value: the chain's output must equal the fround of (layer count + 1) / 1024.
The README reports 54 to 55 µs per evaluation at 64 layers, 64 to 65 µs at 1,024 and 210 to 214 µs at 16,384, measured in Bun 1.4.3 on an Apple M5 Max at a load average of about 4.

sources.label: lab/runtime-cost/README.md line 13
sources.quote: In Bun 1.4.3 on an Apple M5 Max, at a load average of about 4: 54 to 55 µs per evaluation in 64 layers, 64 to 65 µs in 1,024 and 210 to 214 µs in 16,384

claims.claim: The README puts the layer cost at about 10 µs per 1,000 layers.

A local run of the probe on an Apple M4 Max at load about 9 (not a repo result) gave about 67, 77 and 250 µs for the three layer counts; the slope stayed near 10 µs per 1,000 layers, but the absolute numbers moved.

The docs attribute the layer cost to copying values, but copy volume is the same in all three shapes, so the cost that grows is fixed work per layer. This is our inference from the code; the lab does not test it.

sources.label: docs/patterns.md line 7
sources.quote: for copying the values that it reads and the results that it writes

claims.claim: The lab's status page records an earlier executor at 16,384 layers taking 709 µs, and 250 µs after the executor changed how each layer's outputs are copied.
The status figure suggests the per-layer cost is real and not just a fit to the README numbers. This is our inference from one historical measurement, not a tested result.

sources.label: lab/status.md line 89
sources.quote: an indexed copy of each layer's outputs instead of `set` on a new view

claims.claim: In a local compile of the window manager (not a repo result), the first layer holds 401 operations and the sixth holds 10; the layers are not uniform.
The window manager's layers hold a median of 26.5 operations each.

sources.label: lab/status.md line 34
sources.quote: Its layers hold a median of 26.5 operations each

claims.claim: In the same local compile, the layers widen again to 133 operations near the end of the circuit (not a repo result).
The window manager pays the per-layer toll 130 times, not 16,384, and that may be part of why the real circuit sits far from the worst case. The lab does not test that link.
On the candidate gallery, one local run of report.ts (not a repo result) gave about 19 µs for the reference, 4.6 for the full array and 3.2 for the reusable evaluator.

The coordinate transform is a four-operation, three-layer circuit with a direct scalar-JS baseline. In one local run (not a repo result) it took about 93 ns for the reference, 78 for the reusable evaluator and 29 for plain scalar JS.

In this one run, reusable beats full array by about 1.53 times on the coordinate transform, 1.46 on the gallery and 1.16 on the window manager. The smallest circuit gains most here, but one run cannot establish a rule.

claims.claim: The harness wraps the reference and full-array runners in select(), which copies the requested roots on each call; the reusable runner is passed in unwrapped.
Part of the measured gap between the reusable and full-array timings may come from that extra copy loop. We have not measured its size.
The README warns that timing several programs in one process can distort later timings, and the report runs its three circuits in one process.

sources.label: lab/runtime-cost/README.md line 11

claims.claim: A standalone run of the window manager alone (one local run, not a repo result) gave about 47 µs against about 43 in the shared run, which is within noise, so it neither confirms nor refutes the warning.
